prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The first three frames place the wire basket and its contents directly in front of and below the camera, roughly 0.3–0.8 m away, with the counter/display behind them at about 1–2 m; the wearer’s hand in frame 3 is within arm’s reach and partly occludes the basket. Across frames 1–3, the basket shifts left and changes angle as the camera turns, while the depth map preserves a nearer basket rim against more distant surfaces despite RGB motion blur. Frames 4–5 show a transition away from the display toward a more open interior: the nearby woman is approximately 1–2 m ahead and slightly right-to-centre, while the other person and background fixtures are several metres farther away. Bright foreground regions and dark background regions make near/far layering easier to see than in the RGB alone, but absolute distances are uncertain and the smooth, bleeding boundaries—especially around the basket, people, and frame edges—make thin objects and occlusions unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: In frames 1–2 the map identifies almost none of the display geometry and labels one small left-side region as scissors, although the RGB context suggests this detection is spatially unreliable; the basket and most packaged objects are omitted. A small partial person mask appears near the lower part of frame 3, indicating something close to the camera and partly out of view, but its correspondence to the visible hand or nearby scene is uncertain. In frame 4, one small person is several metres ahead near the centre-right, while a much larger person mask occupies the right side at roughly 1–2 m, showing that the nearer woman occludes part of the background; by frame 5 she is more centrally visible, with another person farther right and partly occluded by a large right-edge region labelled TV. The masks clarify object separation, overlap, and partial visibility more readily than the RGB, but missed objects, unstable labels, clipped masks, and scale changes make the inferred layout incomplete.
descriptions.pose: No usable body or hand skeleton is detected in frames 1–3 or frame 5, so the map provides no articulated spatial information for the wearer’s nearby hand, the basket, or the people visible at the end. In frame 4, a yellow pose appears on the large near-right person: facial landmarks lie above a roughly horizontal shoulder segment, placing the upper body about 1–2 m ahead and to the right of the camera wearer. The landmark arrangement is broadly consistent with the person facing generally toward the camera, although gaze direction and arm reach cannot be established because the eyes, torso, and limbs are incomplete. The pose map makes the detected person’s face-above-shoulders geometry clearer than the blurred RGB, but the sparse floating points, missing joints, absent hand detections, and lack of temporal continuity make orientation, occlusion, and movement estimates unreliable.
